title: The nth Character
hints: You can't subscript a `String` with an `Int` — you need a `String.Index`.
`index(_:offsetBy:limitedBy:)` returns `nil` instead of crashing when you'd walk past the limit. Also reject negative offsets and `endIndex`.
`guard offset >= 0, let i = text.index(text.startIndex, offsetBy: offset, limitedBy: text.endIndex), i < text.endIndex else { return nil }; return String(text[i])`.
jsBridge: JS gives `str[5]` in O(1) over UTF-16 units, which can split an emoji. Swift **refuses integer subscripts** on `String` because characters have variable width. You walk with `index(_:offsetBy:limitedBy:)`, which makes the O(n) cost visible.

compass.q: JS `str[i]` is O(1) but can return half an emoji. Swift makes it O(n) and correct. Which trade-off would you choose for a text editor?
If you need random access, like highlighting search matches, what's the idiomatic Swift approach: `Array(string)`, storing `String.Index` values, or `NSRange`?
Can you use an index from one string on another string, or on a mutated copy? What happens?
Java's `charAt(i)` returns a UTF-16 unit like JS. Why did Swift decide the ergonomic loss was worth it?
